title: Networking
description: The network around your services: load balancers, proxies, timeouts, connection reuse and certificates.
resumo: Load balancers: L4 forwards connections, L7 reads HTTP; health checks remove failing instances. No sticky sessions — stay stateless.
Behind a proxy, read `X-Forwarded-*` (`server.forward-headers-strategy`), and trust them only from your proxy.
Every network wait needs a limit: connect (short), read (sized), pool — and defaults may be infinite.
Create HTTP clients once and reuse them: pooled keep-alive connections, HTTP/2 multiplexing.
"PKIX path building failed" = untrusted CA: add the issuing CA to a truststore — never trust-all.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** three instances of the API are running, and something has to decide which one gets each request — and stop sending traffic to one that died.

**Concept:** a load balancer spreads requests across healthy instances. Layer 4 (TCP) balancers forward connections without reading them; layer 7 (HTTP) balancers read the request and can route by path, host or header, terminate TLS and retry. Common algorithms: round robin, least connections, and hashing (the same client to the same instance). Health checks remove an instance that stops answering.

**How it works:** in Kubernetes, a Service balances at layer 4 and an Ingress or Gateway at layer 7; in the cloud, both kinds are managed services.
examples.code:
┌───────────────┐
clients ──────▶ │ Load balancer │   health check: GET /actuator/health/readiness every 5 s
                └───────┬───────┘
          ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
          ▼             ▼             ▼
      api (1) ✓     api (2) ✓     api (3) ✗  <- failing checks: no traffic

L4: forwards TCP connections (fast, protocol-agnostic)
L7: reads HTTP — routes /orders and /catalog to different services, terminates TLS
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between a layer 4 and a layer 7 load balancer?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Sticky sessions to keep a stateful application working. Load becomes uneven, and when an instance dies, every user stuck to it loses their session. Make the application stateless and keep the state in Redis or the database.
examples.code:
# WRONG: the session lives in the instance's memory, so users are pinned to it
loadBalancer.stickySessions: true

# RIGHT: any instance can serve any request
spring.session.store-type: redis

subsections.subtitle: Reverse Proxies and Forwarded Headers
subsections.description: What changes when a proxy sits in front of the application.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** behind the load balancer, the application logs the proxy's IP for every user, and the redirects it generates point to `http://` instead of `https://`.

**Concept:** a reverse proxy (nginx, a cloud load balancer, an Ingress controller) receives the client's connection and opens its own connection to the application. The application then sees the proxy's address, and plain HTTP if TLS was terminated at the proxy. The proxy passes the original information in headers: `X-Forwarded-For` (client IP), `X-Forwarded-Proto` (http or https), `X-Forwarded-Host`, or the standard `Forwarded` header.

**How it works:** tell Spring Boot to read them with `server.forward-headers-strategy`, and only trust them when they come from your own proxy.
examples.code:
client ──HTTPS──▶ proxy (TLS ends here) ──HTTP──▶ application
                  adds: X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7
                        X-Forwarded-Proto: https
                        X-Forwarded-Host: api.shop.com

# application.yml
server:
  forward-headers-strategy: framework     # use X-Forwarded-* to rebuild the original request

request.getRemoteAddr()      // 203.0.113.7 (the client), not the proxy
request.getScheme()          // "https"
examples.interview_question: Why does an application behind a reverse proxy need forwarded headers?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Not configuring forwarded headers behind a TLS-terminating proxy. The application thinks every request is plain HTTP, so it builds `http://` links and redirects (OAuth2 login fails with a redirect URI mismatch, and browsers warn about mixed content).
examples.code:
# WRONG: no configuration behind the proxy
Location: http://api.shop.com/login/oauth2/code/google    <- should be https

# RIGHT
server.forward-headers-strategy: framework

subsections.subtitle: Timeouts: Connect, Read and Pool
subsections.description: Bounding every wait on the network.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a slow dependency makes your threads wait forever, and your service stops answering too.

**Concept:** an HTTP client has several waits, each needing its own limit. The connect timeout bounds opening the TCP connection (short: a few hundred milliseconds to a couple of seconds). The read (or response) timeout bounds waiting for data once connected — longer, sized to the dependency's normal latency. With a connection pool, the time to get a connection from the pool is a third wait. Some clients wait forever by default.

**How it works:** set them on every client: HTTP, database, Redis, Kafka. The total time you can wait must fit inside the time your own caller will wait.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between a connect timeout and a read timeout?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Trusting the default. `java.net.http.HttpClient` has no request timeout unless you set one, and other clients have very long or infinite defaults — one hung dependency then holds a thread forever.

subsections.subtitle: Keep-Alive and HTTP Connection Pools
subsections.description: Reusing connections instead of opening new ones.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** each call to another service spends more time opening a connection and negotiating TLS than doing the actual request.

**Concept:** opening a connection costs a TCP handshake plus, for HTTPS, a TLS handshake — several round trips. HTTP keep-alive reuses one connection for many requests, and HTTP clients keep a pool of open connections per host. HTTP/2 goes further and multiplexes many concurrent requests over one connection.

**How it works:** create one client per target service and reuse it everywhere (in Spring, a bean); size its pool for the concurrency you expect.
examples.interview_question: Why should an HTTP client be created once and reused?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Creating a new HTTP client for every request. No connection is reused, every call pays the TCP and TLS handshakes, and under load the machine can run out of ephemeral ports (closed connections linger in TIME_WAIT).

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a call to an internal service fails with `PKIX path building failed`, and the first answer found online is to "trust all certificates".

**Concept:** Java checks server certificates against its truststore (the JDK's `cacerts`, with the public CAs). A certificate signed by an internal company CA, or a self-signed one, is not trusted until its CA is added. You can add it to a truststore and point the JVM at it, or — in Spring Boot 3.1+ — configure SSL bundles. Certificates expire, so their expiry dates must be monitored.

**How it works:** add the issuing CA, not the server's own certificate, so renewals keep working.
examples.code:
# Inspect the server's chain
$ openssl s_client -connect payments.internal:8443 -showcerts </dev/null

# Add the company CA to a truststore
$ keytool -importcert -alias company-ca -file company-ca.pem \
          -keystore truststore.p12 -storetype PKCS12 -storepass changeit

# Spring Boot SSL bundle (3.1+)
spring:
  ssl:
    bundle:
      pem:
        company:
          truststore:
            certificate: classpath:company-ca.pem
examples.interview_question: What does "PKIX path building failed" mean, and how do you fix it properly?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Disabling certificate validation to make the error go away. A trust-all TrustManager (or `curl -k` in scripts) accepts any certificate, so anyone between the services can impersonate the server and read or change the traffic. Trust the right CA instead.
